title: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Higher taxonomic ranks are almost arbitrary

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The relative value of groups such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families and genera is, at least at present, almost arbitrary, as shown by groups being raised in rank merely because more allied species were discovered.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Finally, with respect to the comparative value of the various groups of species, such as orders, sub-orders, families, sub-families, and genera, they seem to be, at least at present, almost arbitrary.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “Rules and difficulties in classification, explained on the theory of descent with modification”. Scope: taxonomic ranks above the species level

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-04: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rank instability and determinants are empirically measurable. The central judgment that ranks are arbitrary remains partly conceptual, and modern taxonomic practice differs from Darwin's period.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Measure variation among taxonomic authorities and through time in rank assignments for equivalent clades, and test whether added species richness predicts rank elevation independent of clade age or divergence. High instability supports arbitrariness, though no dataset can define how much instability counts as 'almost arbitrary.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Historical taxonomic versions are not uniformly digitized.

Arbitrariness is a normative concept without a unique threshold.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Rank, clade age and richness are standard variables, and massive overlap within a rank versus a clean age band is a concrete confirming or refuting pattern. Time-calibrated trees and a global taxonomy already contain those variables for most named higher taxa. The analysis is a short one; the remaining softness is the vague word 'almost', not missing data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For genera, families and orders, measure the spread of crown ages, species richness and morphological disparity within each rank, and test whether ranks occupy distinct, non-overlapping bands. The claim is confirmed if within-rank spreads dwarf the differences between adjacent ranks, and refuted if a rank consistently marks a similar age or amount of difference across classes.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Some rank changes really do follow the discovery of more allied species, but the historical revision record is less complete than the current ages.

'Almost arbitrary' has no sharp numerical cutoff, so a weak average rise in age from genus to order can be read either way.

Ranks are more nearly commensurate inside one class than they are across animals and plants together.
